articles.headline: OFAC Designates Entities Under Protecting American Intellectual Property Act of 2022, Issues General Licenses
body: The Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) today announced new designations under the Protecting American Intellectual Property Act of 2022 (PAIPA). These actions are accompanied by the issuance of associated General Licenses.

Further details regarding the specific entities designated and the scope of the new general licenses are expected to clarify the impact on various sectors involved in intellectual property and technology transfer.
This move underscores the U.S. government's continued commitment to safeguarding American intellectual property against theft and illicit acquisition globally.

articles.headline: OFAC Amends Venezuela-Related General License and Issues New FAQ
body: The Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) has issued an amended Venezuela-related General License, alongside a new Frequently Asked Question (FAQ).
This amendment and FAQ aim to provide updated guidance and clarity regarding authorized transactions and activities involving Venezuela, potentially impacting specific sectors or entities.
Stakeholders involved in Venezuela-related trade and financial dealings are advised to review the updated guidance to ensure ongoing compliance with U.S. sanctions regulations.

articles.headline: OFAC Imposes New Sanctions on Iran and Cuba, Issues New and Amended General Licenses
body: The Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) has announced new designations targeting entities and individuals related to Iran and Cuba. These actions are accompanied by the issuance of new and amended General Licenses, as well as updated Frequently Asked Questions.
These measures are expected to further tighten financial and trade restrictions on both nations, impacting various sectors including shipping, energy trading, and financial services.
Compliance departments in global banks, insurers, and shipping companies are advised to reassess their exposure to entities in Iran and Cuba in light of these new sanctions.

articles.headline: OFAC Removes Venezuela-Related Designation
body: The Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) has announced the removal of a Venezuela-related designation.
This action indicates a potential recalibration of sanctions policy concerning specific entities or individuals previously targeted under the Venezuela sanctions program.
The removal may ease certain restrictions for the delisted party and could signal broader shifts in U.S. foreign policy towards Venezuela.

articles.headline: OFAC Imposes Counter Narcotics and Counter Terrorism Designations
body: The Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) today announced new designations targeting individuals and entities involved in counter narcotics and counter terrorism activities.
These designations aim to disrupt illicit financial networks and operations that support drug trafficking and terrorist organizations globally.
The action reinforces the U.S. government's ongoing efforts to combat transnational criminal organizations and their facilitators.

articles.headline: OFAC Announces Settlement with Pegasus Worldwide Logistics, Designates International Criminal Court Officials, and Removes Burma-Related Designation
body: The Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) has announced a settlement agreement with Pegasus Worldwide Logistics. Concurrently, OFAC has designated officials of the International Criminal Court and issued associated General Licenses.
In a separate action, OFAC also announced the removal of a Burma-related designation, indicating a targeted adjustment to its sanctions program concerning Myanmar.
These diverse actions highlight OFAC's multi-faceted approach to sanctions enforcement, targeting various illicit activities and adjusting existing regimes as deemed appropriate.

articles.headline: OFAC Issues New Russia-Related General License
body: The Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) has issued a new Russia-related General License.
This new license provides specific authorizations for certain transactions or activities that would otherwise be prohibited under existing Russia sanctions programs.
Entities engaged in Russia-related business should review the details of this new General License to understand its scope and any potential impact on their operations.

articles.headline: OFAC Imposes Iran-Related Designations, Issues New Iran-Related and Amended Russia-Related General Licenses
body: The Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) has announced new Iran-related designations, alongside the issuance of a new Iran-related General License and an amended Russia-related General License.

These actions target Iran's petroleum sector and its network of vessels used to transport oil and petrochemical products, with the State Department also sanctioning additional vessels, entities, and individuals.

The amended Russia-related General License suggests adjustments to existing authorizations, while the new Iran-related license may provide specific carve-outs for certain transactions despite the broader designations.

articles.headline: OFAC Announces Designations Removals and Updates, Publishes Iran-Related Alert and Amended FAQ
body: The Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) has announced several designations removals and updates to its sanctions lists. Concurrently, OFAC has published an Iran-related alert and an amended Iran-related Frequently Asked Question (FAQ).

The alert warns foreign financial institutions about increased sanctions risks for conducting business with Iran or its financial sector, emphasizing that they may face sanctions without advance notice.
This guidance underscores OFAC's continued focus on disrupting Iran's access to the international financial system and advises institutions to review and terminate any such activities.

articles.headline: Bank of America Settles with OFAC for $11,662,930 in Sanctions Violations
body: Bank of America, N.A. has agreed to a settlement with the U.S. Department of the Treasury's Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) for $11,662,930. The settlement resolves 475 apparent violations of multiple sanctions programs, including those targeting Iran, Russia, narcotics, and global terrorism.

The apparent violations occurred due to a combination of technical and human errors, including channeling correspondent banking payments through blocked banks, allowing designated individuals to transact due to poor sanctions alert calibration, and failing to promptly update watchlists.
OFAC determined that the violations were non-egregious and largely not voluntarily self-disclosed, with no reduction to the base penalty for remedial measures or cooperation.

articles.headline: Pegasus Worldwide Logistics Pays $175,015 to Settle OFAC Sanctions Violations
body: Pegasus Worldwide Logistics has reached a settlement agreement with the U.S. Department of the Treasury's Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC), agreeing to pay $175,015.
The settlement addresses apparent violations of OFAC sanctions regulations, though specific details of the violations were not immediately released.
This enforcement action underscores OFAC's continued vigilance in ensuring compliance with U.S. sanctions programs across various industries.

articles.headline: Individual Settles with OFAC for $1,427,230 in Sanctions Violations
body: An individual has agreed to pay $1,427,230 to settle apparent violations of U.S. sanctions regulations with the Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC).
The details of the individual's violations were not immediately specified, but the substantial penalty indicates serious breaches of sanctions compliance.
This action serves as a reminder that OFAC enforcement extends to individuals, not just corporate entities, for non-compliance with sanctions laws.

articles.headline: Rice Lake Weighing Systems, Inc. Pays $60,764 for OFAC Sanctions Violations

While the specific nature of the violations was not detailed, the settlement highlights the importance of robust compliance programs for all companies, regardless of size or industry.
This penalty reinforces OFAC's commitment to enforcing sanctions across a broad spectrum of entities involved in international trade.

articles.headline: Federal Reserve Beige Book Reports Modest Inflation, Rising Energy Costs
body: The Federal Reserve's latest Beige Book report, compiled on or before October 5, 2026, indicates that economic activity expanded slightly in some districts, with overall modest inflation. However, several regions noted sharp increases in home heating oil prices, raising concerns for the upcoming winter.

Consumer-facing firms reported tighter profit margins as price-sensitive customers resisted price hikes, leading businesses to manage margins through selective increases, targeted incentives, and cost-reducing menu changes.

Persistent uncertainty surrounding energy and tariffs is expected to lead to further price increases in the coming months as existing contracts expire and firms renegotiate input and delivery contracts.

articles.headline: OCC Imposes Record $750 Million Penalty on Bank of America for BSA/AML Failures
body: The Office of the Comptroller of the Currency (OCC) has announced a record $750 million civil money penalty against Bank of America, N.A. for widespread and egregious violations of the Bank Secrecy Act (BSA) and its implementing regulations.

The OCC found that Bank of America's BSA/AML compliance program was deficient and ineffective, with a transaction monitoring system that failed to properly monitor trillions of dollars in transactions. This led to numerous late suspicious activity reports (SARs) involving billions of dollars.

This action, the largest in OCC history, was taken in coordination with the Financial Crimes Enforcement Network (FinCEN), which assessed a $1.2 billion penalty against the bank, crediting the OCC's fine.

articles.headline: Streamlining Export Controls for Drone Exports
body: The Bureau of Industry and Security (BIS) is easing export controls on certain Unmanned Aerial Vehicles (UAVs or drones) and related parts, components, accessories, attachments, technology, and software under the Export Administration Regulations (EAR). Specifically, this rule: eliminates wind gust tolerance as a parameter for determining UAV controls under the EAR; increases the threshold for national security controls on certain UAVs from an endurance of 30 minutes to an endurance of 3 hours; makes conforming changes to remove national security controls on software and technology associated with UAVs with an endurance less than 3 hours; maintains military end-use and end-user controls on those lower endurance drones and associated software and technology; clarifies Commerce Control List (CCL) controls for certain UAVs specially designed for military use; and removes national security controls on certain specially designed parts, components, accessories, and attachments for such UAVs as they do not provide any significant military or intelligence capabilities.

articles.headline: Implementation of EAR Export Controls on Silencers, Mufflers, and Sound Suppressors; and Other Firearms Related Changes
body: The Department of Commerce (Commerce), Bureau of Industry and Security (BIS) is revising the Export Administration Regulations (EAR) and the Commerce Control List (CCL) to appropriately control certain silencers, mufflers, and sound suppressors (sound suppressors) that will no longer be described on the International Traffic in Arms Regulations U.S. Munitions List (USML). This interim final rule (IFR) complements a Department of State interim final rule published elsewhere in this issue of the Federal Register (International Traffic in Arms Regulations: USML Category I Firearm Suppressors (1400-AG11) (State IFR)). This transfer of jurisdiction will reduce the regulatory burden on exports of sound suppressors. This IFR also revises the EAR to allow firearms and related items to be temporarily exported and reexported under a license exception as tools of trade, thereby relieving exporters of the regulatory burden of applying for authorization. Finally, this IFR clarifies which items fall within the scope of the EAR's entry clearance requirements for a temporary import.

articles.headline: Enhanced Favorable Treatment for the United Arab Emirates Under the Export Administration Regulations
body: In this final rule, the Bureau of Industry and Security (BIS) amends the Export Administration Regulations (EAR) to provide enhanced favorable treatment for the United Arab Emirates (UAE). Specifically, BIS is removing the UAE from Country Groups D:3 and D:4 and adding the UAE to Country Group A:5. More license exceptions will now be available, including Strategic Trade Authorization (STA) for the UAE Government and approved commercial entities in the UAE. STA will authorize the export, reexport, or transfer (in-country) of military items; certain commercial satellites and spacecraft; and dual-use items useful in, inter alia, oil and gas production, desalination, and civil nuclear power generation. The UAE Government and approved commercial entities will also have license-free access to advanced computing items, consistent with the May 2025 U.S.-UAE Artificial Intelligence Cooperation framework, without compromising U.S. digital infrastructure buildout.
